name: Generac Guardian 22kW
summary: Where outages run long and often, nothing else on this list can stand in for an automatic standby unit.
verdict: For a household that wants the power back without anyone stepping outside, the Guardian 22kW is the standard answer. It is mounted permanently on a pad, piped to natural gas or a propane tank and wired through an automatic transfer switch, so it detects the outage, starts and carries the house without help. Generac rates it at 22,000 watts on propane and 19,500 on natural gas, enough for a typical 2,000 to 3,000 square foot home with a central air conditioner and gas heat, particularly with the load-shedding modules Generac sells. The air-cooled engine runs a weekly self-exercise and reports its status to the Mobile Link app. The drawbacks are cost and paperwork: the unit alone is roughly $5,500 to $6,500 at the time of writing, and permits, electrical work, gas piping and the pad commonly bring the installed total to $10,000 to $18,000 or more. Budget for yearly oil, filter and plug service from a dealer.
skipIf: Installed cost commonly runs well into five figures

name: Generac GP8000E
summary: Plenty of running watts for the money from a brand with broad parts and service coverage.
verdict: Choose the GP8000E when you want large portable output and are happy to run on gasoline. Generac rates it at 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts, enough for a 240V well pump, a refrigerator, a freezer, a furnace blower and lights through a transfer switch, or a window air conditioner in place of one of those. Electric start works from a key switch with a pull cord as backup, and the COsense module stops the engine if carbon monoxide gathers around it. The open frame and steel cradle are made to be hauled out of a shed, and the never-flat wheels help on gravel. Because it is a conventional generator rather than an inverter, the engine holds a fixed speed, so fuel burn and noise barely fall at light load. Set aside money for stabilized gasoline and approved cans. Expect roughly $1,000 to $1,300 at the time of writing.

name: DuroMax XP12000EH
summary: The portable that gets closest to standby output, for buyers willing to live with the weight, noise and fuel burn.
verdict: The XP12000EH is close to the most generator most people would still call portable. DuroMax rates it at 12,000 starting and 9,500 running watts on gasoline, with lower figures on propane, and it has a 50-amp 120/240V outlet suited to a larger manual transfer switch or a panel interlock. That can run a central air conditioner in the smaller tonnage ranges alongside essentials, depending on its starting draw, or carry much of a house that has gas heat and a gas water heater. The compromises are physical. At well over 200 pounds it lives on its wheels, and at heavy load it burns many gallons of gasoline a day or needs a serious propane supply. If you are shopping at this size, get a price on a small standby unit as well; the gap shrinks once fuel, cans and labor are counted. Expect roughly $1,200 to $1,600 at the time of writing.

name: Westinghouse WGen9500 Remote-Start
summary: The value choice when you want headroom for a window air conditioner or a larger well pump beyond the essentials.
verdict: The WGen9500 delivers a lot of gasoline generator for its price. Westinghouse rates it at 9,500 running and 12,500 starting watts, one step above the 8,000-watt class, which leaves room for a window air conditioner or a bigger well pump on top of the usual essentials. Key-fob remote start is genuinely handy in bad weather, and the outlet panel carries both a 30-amp and a 50-amp 120/240V locking outlet, so it can feed either common size of transfer switch or inlet. The 6.6-gallon tank has a fuel gauge, and Westinghouse lists a long run time at moderate load. It is heavy enough that you will lean on the wheels and handle, and at high loads it goes through gasoline quickly. Newer production adds a carbon monoxide sensor; check that the unit you buy has it. Expect roughly $1,100 to $1,500 at the time of writing.

name: Firman P08004 Gas Portable
summary: A sound route to 8,000 running watts when price matters more than features.
verdict: Firman's P08004 is a plain, no-frills way into the 8,000-watt class. On gasoline it is rated at 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts, the same headline numbers as the GP8000E, and its 120/240V output can feed a transfer switch or interlock. That handles a well pump or sump pump plus a refrigerator, freezer, furnace blower and lights in a typical house. The frame and wheels are made for rough handling, and the controls are simple. The lower price mostly costs you on support: Firman's service network is thinner than Generac's or Westinghouse's, and the feature list is shorter. Owners commonly report that it starts and runs well when it gets fresh, stabilized fuel and regular exercise. Carbon monoxide shutoff and start type vary by version, so check the specific listing. Expect roughly $800 to $1,100 at the time of writing.

name: DuroMax XP12000E Gasoline Portable
summary: For houses that want near-standby output from a portable and can keep it supplied with fuel.
verdict: The XP12000E is the gasoline-only version of DuroMax's large portable, rated at 9,500 running and 12,000 starting watts. In some cases that is enough for a modest central air conditioner, particularly with a soft-start kit, or for a big share of a house with gas heat and a gas water heater. A 50-amp 120/240V outlet suits a larger transfer switch or panel interlock. Power comes from a 457cc engine with electric start, and the alternator uses copper windings. All that output brings weight of well over 200 pounds, noise, and fuel burn that can reach many gallons a day under heavy load. If you are weighing one, run the fuel math first and compare its total cost with a small standby generator on natural gas; for some homes the standby comes out ahead once fuel and labor are counted. Expect roughly $1,100 to $1,500 at the time of writing.

name: DuroMax XP13000HXT Tri Fuel Portable Generator with CO Alert
summary: The pick for houses already on a natural gas line that want multi-day run time without hauling fuel.
verdict: Tri fuel adds natural gas to gasoline and propane, and for houses already plumbed for gas it changes the math of a long outage completely. Instead of swapping cylinders every few hours, a properly installed quick-connect lets the generator run from the utility line for as long as gas pressure holds. DuroMax's spec sheet rates the XP13000HXT at 13,000 peak and 10,500 running watts on gasoline, 12,000 peak and 9,500 running on propane, and 10,000 peak and 8,500 running on natural gas. That natural gas figure is still enough for a large share of a house through a transfer switch. DuroMax lists half-load run time of 8.5 hours on gasoline and 6.5 hours on propane. The HXT adds DuroMax's CO Alert technology, which shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide accumulates, and push-button starting. The caveats: natural gas connection is plumbing work, and DuroMax specifies a supply pressure range that a long run of small pipe may not meet, so have a plumber check it. Retail listings vary on stock, so confirm the exact model number in the listing before you buy.
